blocks.text: Space is said to be a three-dimensional extent in which all objects and events occur. It provides a framework to define the position and motion of various objects under the influence of some force.

Time measures the sequence and duration of events. In the theory of relativity time is not absolute; it is considered the fourth dimension. For example, oscillatory motion, such as that of a swinging pendulum, relies on time to determine the frequency of oscillation. Another example is time dilation, discussed earlier in this chapter, in which time passes more slowly for an observer moving at extremely high speed compared with one at rest. The special theory of relativity shows that space and time are related to each other; it describes how space and time are influenced by gravity and speed, such as the bending of light round massive objects like stars.

blocks.title: Space-time
blocks.text: Space-time is a mathematical model that unifies space and time into a single continuum. It is used to describe all points of space and time and their relation to each other. It can be pictured as a sheet that can bend; its bending gives effects such as the stretching and compression seen when gravitational waves pass through objects.

According to Einstein's theory, space-time is curved, especially near massive bodies and for speeds approaching the speed of light. We can visualize this as a fabric sheet: if a heavy ball is placed on the sheet, it curves (Fig. 11.2). Objects such as stars and planets cause space-time to curve around themselves, much as an elastic fabric deforms when holding a ball; the more massive the object, the deeper the curve. Consequently we do not speak of a force of gravity acting on bodies; instead we say that bodies and light rays move along geodesics (analogous to straight lines in plane geometry) in curved space-time. Thus a body at rest or moving slowly near a massive object follows a geodesic towards that object.

blocks.text: Einstein's theory provides a physical picture of how gravity works. Newton discovered the inverse-square law of gravity but stated explicitly that he offered no explanation of why gravity should follow this law. Einstein's theory also describes gravity as following an inverse-square law (except in strong gravitational fields), but it explains why. That is why Einstein's theory is considered an advance over Newton's, even though it includes Newton's theory and gives the same results in all but very strong gravitational fields.

The bending of starlight by the Sun's gravity was measured during a solar eclipse in 1919. The results matched Einstein's theory rather than Newton's, and Einstein's theory was hailed as a scientific triumph. Light from a star A is deflected as it passes close to the Sun on its way to the Earth, so we see the star in the apparent direction B, shifted by an angle phi; Einstein predicted phi = 1.745 seconds of arc, and the same value was found in the 1919 eclipse (Interesting Information). Another success of Einstein's theory was the detection of gravitational waves, produced by some celestial events that cause disturbances (squeezes and stretches) in the curvature of space-time; they were detected in 2015 and announced in 2016.

blocks.text: Let a spaceship travel to a star at half the speed of light, taking eight years to reach it from the point of view of an observer on the Earth. From the Earth's point of view the clocks on the spaceship run slowly, so less time passes on the spaceship than on the Earth. For the occupants of the spaceship the length of the journey has contracted, and they cover it in less time: they record 7 years rather than 8. The faster you move, or the closer you are to a strong source of gravity, the slower time goes for you (For Your Information); a spaceship moving extremely fast near a black hole, as in the film 'Interstellar', could miss 7 years on the Earth for every hour (Interesting Information).
